new_statements.citation: Wannemacher, Mark. 2011. A Phonological Overview of the Lacid Language. Research Project RU 11. Chiang Mai: Linguistics Institute, Payap University.
new_statements.locator: §3.1 Syllable and Word Structure, p. 6 (pdf p. 11); §3.3.2 rule (16), p. 12 (pdf p. 17); §3.5.1 Tone Inventory and Description, p. 14 (pdf p. 19)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lacid/Lashi is a tone language (three contrastive tones in open/nasal-final syllables, two in checked syllables, plus a stiff/slack voice-quality contrast); the source posits no word-stress contrast and gives no positional stress rule. The only stress statement is that in (mostly bisyllabic) words the word-initial CV syllable can be unstressed, in which case its vowel reduces to [ə] and it loses contrastive tone, taking its pitch from the following syllable — i.e. the sesquisyllabic pattern with prominence on the final (major) syllable, the initial minor syllable being unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Reduced-syllable tone assimilation can fail when a voiceless consonant intervenes (e.g. jə³.tʰoŋ⁵ ‘farm’). Which vowels reduce in unstressed initial syllables is undetermined ('not sufficient data'). Wannemacher's own list of areas for further study includes 'the initial unstressed CV syllable' (p. 19). Second-hand (Morse 1960 ms., reported on p. 5): on /ʔ/-final syllables 'words with stress' carry high tone and 'unstressed words' low tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word (citation forms elicited in isolation and in a tone frame from a 756-item wordlist; mono-/bisyllabic words and compounds up to four syllables). No phrase-level or intonational stress described.
new_statements.identity_note: Wannemacher 2011 describes the Lacid of the Waimo area, eastern Kachin State, Myanmar (three male speakers, 1994); Luk 2017 describes Myanmar Lacid (thesis supported by the Lacid Language and Culture Committee). Glottolog has no dialect-level codes under lash1243; the Chinese-side variety is called Leqi (勒期语) in Dai's works. No differently named variety is involved.

sources.note: Tone language: 3 tones (high-fall, high-mid, low) in unchecked syllables, 2 (high, low) in checked syllables, plus stiff/slack voice. Stress is mentioned only for the word-initial reduced presyllable: 'a reduced presyllable Cə which can occur in unstressed initial CV syllables' (§3.1 p.6); vowel reduction rule (16) 'vowel ---> ə in an open, unstressed, word initial CV syllable' (§3.3.2 p.12); 'Tone in reduced syllables is non-contrastive and tends to assimilate to the tone of the following syllable' (§3.5.1 p.14); 'Reduced syllables do not carry contrastive tone' (§4.3 p.18). sources.citation: Luk, Hkaw. 2017. A Grammatical Sketch of Lacid. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai (advisor Larin Adams; chair Nathan W. Hill). xvi+183 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Brief phonology (ch. 3, pp. 13-17): three phonemic pitch-based tones (high, mid, low) plus creaky vs non-creaky voice (p.16); syllable C1(C2)V1(V2)(C3), two syllabic nasals and 'a reduced presyllable Cə' (p.16); words mostly mono- or bisyllabic, up to four syllables. The words stress/accent/prominence do not occur anywhere in the thesis (grep of full text).

sources.citation: Sawada, Hideo. n.d. 'Lacid', in Languages of the Kachin region, ILCAA Kachin portal (online sketch: sounds/orthography, word formation, grammar, vocabulary).
sources.note: 'Lacid is a tone language where tonal distinctions play an important role to distinguish words'; four tones (falling, low, high, high-falling) illustrated on /o/; tones and final glottal stop written with syllable-final signs. Nothing on stress.
